question: A 25-year-old tribal labourer from Odisha presents with 4 days of high-grade fever, rigors, and confusion. Peripheral blood smear shows P. falciparum trophozoites. Blood glucose is 42 mg/dL. He is drowsy but rousable. What is the most appropriate initial management?

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Oral ACT is appropriate for uncomplicated P. falciparum malaria. This patient has altered consciousness and hypoglycaemia — features of severe malaria requiring parenteral therapy, not oral.

answers.text: IV artesunate (2.4 mg/kg at 0, 12, 24 hours, then daily) plus correction of hypoglycaemia with IV dextrose

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. Severe malaria (altered consciousness, hypoglycaemia, haemoglobin <7, respiratory distress, parasitaemia >5%) requires IV artesunate — the WHO/NVBDCP recommended first-line parenteral agent. Hypoglycaemia in severe malaria (due to parasite glucose consumption and quinine-induced hyperinsulinaemia) must be corrected immediately with IV 25–50% dextrose. Artemether IM is an acceptable alternative if IV artesunate is unavailable.

answers.text: IV quinine infusion as first-line for severe malaria

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: IV quinine was previously first-line for severe malaria but has been superseded by IV artesunate, which has superior efficacy and a better safety profile (less hypoglycaemia). Quinine is now a reserve alternative when artesunate is unavailable.
Chloroquine resistance in P. falciparum is widespread in India. Chloroquine is effective only for P. vivax and P. malariae — NOT P. falciparum. This patient requires IV artesunate.

overallFeedback.feedback: Severe P. falciparum malaria = IV artesunate (NVBDCP first-line). Immediately correct hypoglycaemia. Chloroquine does not cover P. falciparum; IV quinine is the reserve only when artesunate is unavailable.

Excellent. NVBDCP (India 2025) treatment for severe P. falciparum malaria: IV artesunate is first-line. Remember the 6 features of severe malaria: cerebral malaria, severe anaemia, respiratory distress, hypoglycaemia, renal failure, and hyperparasitaemia (>5%).
